content: Centella asiatica, commonly known as Gotu Kola, is a small herbaceous annual plant belonging to the Apiaceae family, which also includes carrots and dill. It is native to regions such as northern Australia, New Guinea, Melanesia, Malaysia, Iran, and other parts of Asia. The plant is also referred to by various names, including Asiatic Pennywort, Luei Gong Gen, Antanan, Pegaga, Kula kud, and Brahmi, although the latter name is shared with other herbs like Bacopa monnieri. It has been traditionally used as a medicinal herb in both Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine. Its botanical synonyms include Hydrocotyle asiatica L. and Trisanthus cochinchinensis (Lour.). Description Stem The stems of Centella asiatica are slender, creeping stolons that are green to reddish-green in color. These stolons interconnect individual plants. The plant has long-stalked, green, reniform (kidney-shaped) leaves with rounded apices. The leaves have a smooth texture and display palmate venation. They are borne on periclade petioles, which are approximately 20 cm in length. The rootstock consists of vertically growing rhizomes that are cream-colored and covered with root hairs. Flowers The flowers of Centella asiatica are small and range in color from pinkish to red. They grow in small, rounded clusters (umbels) near the soil surface. Each flower is partially enclosed by two green bracts. The hermaphroditic flowers are minute, measuring less than 3 mm, and have 5–6 corolla lobes. Each flower contains five stamens and two styles. The fruit of the plant is densely reticulate, which differentiates it from species of Hydrocotyle that have smooth, ribbed, or warty fruit. The plant matures within three months, and the entire plant, including its roots, is harvested manually. Habitat Centella asiatica thrives in low, wet areas such as along ditches. In regions like India and Southeast Asia, the plant is often subject to high levels of bacterial contamination, likely due to being harvested from sewage ditches. As an aquatic plant, it is particularly sensitive to water pollutants, which can easily be absorbed into the plant. Culinary Uses In Sri Lankan cuisine, Centella asiatica is used as a leafy green and is most commonly prepared as mallung, a traditional accompaniment to rice and curry. Mallung pairs well with vegetarian dishes such as dhal (parippu) and jackfruit or pumpkin curry. The dish is considered highly nutritious and typically includes finely chopped Gotu Kola, grated coconut, and sometimes chilies, lime or lemon juice, dried fish, curry leaves, and spices like fried mustard seeds. Additionally, Centella leaves are used to make a sweet beverage known as the pennywort drink. Medicinal Uses Pharmacology and Constituents Centella asiatica contains two primary active constituents: Bacoside A and Bacoside B. Bacoside A facilitates the release of nitric oxide, which promotes the relaxation of the aorta and veins, enhancing blood flow throughout the body. Bacoside B is a protein that nourishes brain cells. Asiaticosides, another key component, stimulate the reticuloendothelial system, which is involved in the formation of new blood cells, destruction of old ones, storage of fatty materials, iron metabolism, immune responses, and inflammation. Asiaticosides also play a role in connective tissue development, aiding in the healing of ulcers, skin injuries, and other connective tissue damage. They reduce capillary fragility and stimulate keratinization, which is essential for healthy skin. Additionally, these compounds promote the synthesis of lipids and proteins necessary for skin health. Centella asiatica contains a variety of other bioactive compounds, including: Minerals: Calcium, Iron, Selenium, Magnesium Vitamins: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C), Beta Carotene Essential oils: Camphor Triterpenes: Betulinic Acid, Brahmic Acid, Isobrahmic Acid, Thankuniside, Thankunic Acid Saponins: Brahmoside, Asiaticoside A & B, Brahminoside, Madecassoside Flavones: Quercetin Actions Gotu Kola exhibits a range of pharmacological actions, including mild adaptogenic, antibacterial, antiviral, anti-inflammatory, anti-ulcerogenic, anxiolytic, cerebral tonic, circulatory stimulant, diuretic, nervine, and vulnerary (wound-healing) properties. Medicinal Uses and Studies When consumed raw as a salad leaf, Gotu Kola is believed to help maintain youthfulness. In Thailand, it is commonly consumed as an afternoon pick-me-up. A decoction of the leaf juice is thought to alleviate hypertension and is also used as a general health tonic. A poultice made from the leaves is applied to open sores. Interestingly, chewing the plant for extended periods can induce entheogenic meditation, similar to the effects of Salvia divinorum, though this practice is considered dangerous as it may cause temporomandibular joint pain. In 1979, Richard Lucas claimed in a book that a subspecies of Centella asiatica, referred to as Hydrocotyle asiatica minor or Fo ti tieng, contained a longevity factor called Youth Vitamin X, which was purported to act as a tonic for the brain and endocrine glands. However, master herbalist Michael Moore has stated that no such subspecies or vitamin exists. Despite this, some of the cerebral circulatory and dermatological benefits attributed to Centella asiatica have been substantiated by scientific studies. Several studies have documented the plant's ability to aid wound healing, which is one reason for its traditional use in treating leprosy. Treatment with Centella asiatica has been shown to stimulate scar maturation through the production of type I collagen. It also significantly reduces inflammatory reactions and myofibroblast production. Isolated steroids from the plant have been used in leprosy treatment. Preliminary evidence also suggests potential nootropic effects, enhancing cognitive function. Centella asiatica is used to revitalize the brain and nervous system, improve attention span and concentration, and combat aging. It also possesses antioxidant properties and is effective in treating venous insufficiency. In Thailand, it is used for opium detoxification. Folklore Gotu Kola features in the longevity myth of Tai Chi Chuan master Li Ching-Yun, who reportedly lived to the age of 256, partly due to his use of traditional Chinese herbs, including Gotu Kola. A Sri Lankan folklore tale recounts the story of a 10th-century king named Aruna, who claimed that Gotu Kola provided him with the energy and stamina to satisfy his 50-woman harem.
